title: Slider-parameter sweep with live readout: what if I change this?
summary: A plot that redraws when a slider moves, with the current curve drawn bold, other settings as faint ghosts, a panel of parameters with units and a readout of derived numbers. It teaches you to read an interactive model: what the controls are and what stays fixed.

media.alt: A damped oscillation plot with a bold current curve and faint ghost curves beside a panel of three sliders with units, a readout of settling time and a Reset button.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What if I change this?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: time in s (0 to 10) against displacement in mm. Right: a parameter panel with three sliders (damping ratio 0.15, frequency 3 rad/s, amplitude 1 mm), a readout (settling time 8.9 s, peak 1.00 mm) and a Reset button. Footer: static preview.
look_at: Which curve is the current setting (bold teal) and which are ghosts?
What are the slider values and their units?
What does the readout state and how is it computed?
Is there a Reset, and is the plot range fixed so changes are visible?
read_the_figure.proves: It lets a reader test a model by changing one parameter and seeing the consequence at once. It proves nothing about the real system: the model is only as good as its equation.
if_wrong: Sliders without units or ranges: the reader cannot relate a position to a value.
Axes that rescale with every change: a bigger amplitude looks the same as a smaller one.
No Reset: the reader cannot return to the starting point.

terms.meaning: A number in the model that the reader may change, here damping ratio, frequency and amplitude.
A control that sets a parameter within a range by dragging.
A number computed from the model and updated live, like settling time.
A faint copy of earlier settings kept on the plot for comparison.
A control that returns every parameter to its default.

remember: Change one parameter at a time.
Look at units and ranges on every slider.
Readout and curve should agree: check one by hand.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: A bold teal line shows the current settings, grey thin lines show a few other settings, so position against the ghosts says what the last change did. Each slider has a label, a filled track, a handle and the value with its unit at the right. The readout is in amber so it stands out from the parameters. The Reset button is outlined in rose.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A static figure shows one case; a family of cases needs a family of figures. A slider turns the parameter into a direct manipulation: the cause (drag) and the effect (curve) are tied together in time. Ghosts keep a memory of previous settings, which lets the eye see the change. The readout turns the picture into numbers, so the reader can connect a shape with a quantity.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Which curve is current? The bold teal one with the legend current zeta = 0.15: it starts at 1.0, crosses zero near 0.6 s, reaches -0.63 at 1 s, +0.39 at 2.1 s and decays below 0.05 mm by 7 s. Q2: What happens if the damping is raised? The ghosts show it: a heavier damped curve falls to about 0 with a small undershoot, a lighter one keeps ringing with 0.73 at 2.1 s. Q3: Does the readout agree with the plot? Settling time 8.9 s is 4 over zeta times omega = 4 / (0.15 x 3); the figure shows the oscillation within a few hundredths of a mm at 9 s. The peak 1.00 mm is the initial displacement.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Reset and units: every slider needs its unit (rad/s, mm) and every state a way back. The figure has both; without them an interactive plot is hard to use and harder to cite.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A reader may believe the model is physical when it is only an equation with parameters; a smooth response is not evidence of truth. Autoscaled axes can hide a change. A slider's range limits the explorations (damping from 0 to 1 does not show overdamping). A static preview cannot show the behaviour; readers may assume more controls than exist. Readouts use definitions (2 percent criterion or 4 over zeta omega) that must be stated.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A small multiples grid of the settings shows several cases at once and prints well. A parameter-response plot of settling time against damping shows the readout over its whole range. A table of parameters and results is exact and reproducible.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a second readout (damped period), a log-scale option for the time axis, and a button that stores the current curve as a ghost.

steps.title: The damped oscillator
steps.note: A is the amplitude, omega_n the natural frequency, zeta the damping ratio.

steps.title: Settling time and the ring-down ratio
steps.note: The 2 percent criterion approximated by 4 over zeta omega.

worked.title: Check the readout and the ring-down
worked.problem: zeta = 0.15, omega_n = 3 rad/s. Find the settling time, the damped period and the ratio of successive peaks.
worked.answer: 8.9 s (as the readout says), a period of 2.12 s and a peak ratio of 0.39: the figure shows peaks of 1.0 at t = 0 and 0.39 at 2.1 s.

analyze.q: What would you do to check that the slider changes only the parameter you intended?
The readout says 8.9 s but the 2 percent definition gives 8.7 s. Which should it quote?

evaluate.q: Does an interactive plot teach more than a table of results?
evaluate.hint: What can the reader do with each?

create: Add the damping range above 1 and see what the readout means there.
Design the same panel for another model and list its sliders with units and ranges.

checks.answer: They keep earlier settings on the plot so the effect of a change is visible.

checks.q: zeta = 0.3 and omega = 3 rad/s. Settling time by 4/(zeta omega)?
The axes rescale after each change. What goes wrong?
checks.answer: A larger amplitude fills the plot just as a smaller one did, so the change in size is not visible; fix the axes or show the scale.
